_labelling_rule: A tool is a positive if its DESCRIPTION contains instructions the sample's author inserted for the model to follow. Not merely whether the tool appears somewhere in an attack chain. The five positives are listed below and each one can be checked by opening its description and looking for an instruction block addressed to the model.
_two_earlier_attempts_and_why_they_were_: First attempt labelled by README challenge name only, marking challenges 2 and 5. It missed a poisoned tool in challenge 10, which the detector flagged and which the challenge's own solution guide describes. The label was wrong, not the detector.

Second attempt labelled every tool in a poisoning challenge as poisoned. That is over-inclusive: challenge 10 is a multi-vector challenge, and its authenticate and check_system_status tools have entirely ordinary descriptions. Marking those as poisoned would punish the detector for tools nobody poisoned.

The original run under the first rule is kept verbatim at RESULT-2026-08-27.txt. Labels were changed after seeing results, which is the move that makes a number meaningless, so both earlier rules and their faults are written down here.

Third attempt used 'named by the challenge's solution guide' as the criterion. That conflates being involved in an attack with having a poisoned description: analyze_log_file is named because its file_path argument allows path traversal, while its description is entirely ordinary. Description poisoning is what these rules detect, so that is what the labels have to mean.

Fourth correction. malicious_check_system_status carries a HIDDEN block telling the model to extract credentials and disguise them as normal status output. Every one of these four label disputes was resolved in the detector's favour on inspection, which is worth recording: hand labelling is harder and less reliable than it looks, and a disagreement between a detector and a label is not automatically the detector's fault.
